questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Career opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: As a Human Geographer at UCPH, I am often engaged with issues from the Global South. In order to complement theoretical knowledge with practical experience, I considered it as crucial to gain a deeper understanding of the context by going abroad. South Africa, a country faced with many crises and opportunities, provided an excellent destination.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Stellenbosch University shared information only upon arrival. It would be easier and more convenient to be able to access online platforms prior to the arrival in order to check classroom locations, class sizes, learning materials, etc.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The study abroad team assisted generously with everything a student needed help in (technical, cultural, academic, ... issues). There was an orientation week where international students engaged with each other and the institution, which was very helpful to settle in.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I stayed with Stellies Student Stay, a private company that provides housing for both local and international students. More specifically, I stayed in De Jordaan, a former mansion refurbished to fit 17 students. Depending on the student's own expectations and characteristics, it can either be great fun or challenging. That said, it also depends a lot on the housemates - it should be noted, however, that most times there are at least some (out of the 17) who you can get along with very well. At the same time, you should also always expect that everyone should also expect to have people in the house who they don't really get along with. Overall, it is how you cope with it and how you balance it out. In any case, however, it helps a lot with socializing in the first weeks after arrival. There are always housemates around who want to go on adventures, parties, roadtrips, beach days, etc. And many people in the house often know many more people from their classes, etc. So you won't have any issues with meeting people.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Stellenbosch basically is one huge campus, so even the private accommodations are on campus. And they are much nicer than University accommodations, where you often have to share a room with other people. The private accommodations are more expensive, often even in the European price range, but personally I believe it's worth it to pay more for accommodation and have a nicer room with more personal freedom (there are often quite strict rules in the university residences).

How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Incoming international students have to send a list with courses they'd like to choose. It's often quite convenient when you are choosing generic courses, but the more specialized your UCPH program is, the more difficult it is to enquiry about courses. It is always good to contact the facilitator of the program, if you have any questions about the course content and can't find anything online.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Some more generic guides, but the more specific your program at home, the more likely it is that you have to seek assistance in order to enquire about courses. It helps to contact the International office, or the facilitator of the course. They can mostly help best with any questions regarding topics covered, requirements, etc.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Generally, if UCPH approves your course selection, you don't have any issues of getting accepted to the classes you'd like to register for.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Rather look for more 'hidden' courses that align more with your academic and personal interests, than just going the 'easy' way and register for courses that are sent to you by the International office. Those are often courses that are specifically designed for Exchange students (and if they're interesting to you, then choose them!), but they are not really academically beneficial and you don't meet any locals.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: The course level in my department (the Centre for Sustainability Transitions) was quite high, sometimes even more challenging and demanding than the courses at UCPH. The workload generally is quite high, regardless of your program and in which department / faculty you end up. Stellenbosch University is a fairly demanding institution, and you are often required to attend courses, do a lot of group work, and there are both mid-term exams and final exams.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: My department, the Centre for Sustainability Transitions, has a very unique way of teaching and learning. It is very progressive and focuses on immersive learning experiences, which are very different to more traditional forms of learning and teaching at home. That said, the CST is internationally recognized as a world-class teaching and research hub, so it's not necessarily bad - I would even say it challenges your engrained ways of thinking and opens up your mind in forms you would have never expected. On the other hand, the CST is zero representative of the (often) ultra-conservative patterns within Afrikaans-dominated Stellenbosch University, so if you are studying anything else than some Sustainability-related programs, expect very traditional forms of teaching.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
- Leading Transitions and Socio-Ecological Ethics
- Sustainable Economic Policy Options
- Capita Selecta: Indigenous Knowledges and Sustainable Development
- Development Planning and Environmental Analysis

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The program has changed its courses after I left, so there might be other courses now. If you are studying something Sustainability-related, definitely choose courses at the CST. Otherwise, I can't really help.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: In South Africa, you really have to be aware of your stuff. Don't be careless, otherwise your valuables (phone, wallet, bags) is in great risk of being stolen. This can cost you a new iPad, laptop, phone, wallet - everything happened within the International cohort.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The supermarket is not much cheaper, sometimes even more expensive, than at home. This is quite surprising considering the general very low cost of living in SA. Cooking yourself is still the cheapest in the long-term, but you can go out for lunch for around 30kr - and have a nice lunch even.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are so many societies - from wine society to scuba diving - that you can easily join one of your preference, if you would like to. You have to pay some fees though.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: One simple advice: Go out and explore South Africa, and Southern Africa! Cape Town, Kruger, Botswana, Western Cape, Eastern Cape, Mozambique, etc.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go out and explore! Around Stellenbosch, there are plenty of things to do, from wine tasting to swimming, to hiking.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Stellenbosch University has nothing to do with the rest of South Africa, or Africa for that matter. It feels like a mixture of Australia and USA, with African influences. Outside of Stellenbosch, things are quite different - more diverse, more chaotic, more friendly. It's generally easy to adjust to these new contexts I would say, but that maybe also depends a lot on the subjective experiences.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Choose courses that are not specifically designed for incoming internationals and connect with locals at parties.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The widespread poverty (people living in inhumane conditions in townships), the racial segregation, the inherent racism in the South African system.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The friendly and welcoming nature of people, the diversity, and positivity.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
1. Put life first, university second. 
2. Go out and explore, connect with other people and especially locals. Go beyond the international bubble!
3. Don't be careless, but don't be scared either. A healthy balance makes your trip safe and full of great experiences. Leave your (hopefully very implicit) forms of "White Western hegemony" behind.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Rent a car (with housemates or friends). It makes things so much easier, and it's not really expensive. You can go on roadtrips all the time, go surfing, hiking, swimming, etc. Stellenbosch is quite small and you miss all the beautiful things that are outside of Stellies.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: For me personally the academic experience at CST, but this is very subjective given my focus of studies and unfortunately not everyone has the privilege of studying there given their academic orientation. So, I guess, besides that, it is the natural and cultural beauty of Africa.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To cope with the issues of security, racism, and poverty.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
